decision.explanation: The functions are continuous at π/3, so substitute directly: tan²(π/3)=3 and cot²(π/3)=1/3. Thus the limit is 3+3(1/3)=4.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ directly into the limit, we have

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /3)}({tan}^{2}⁡(x)+3{cot}^{2}⁡(x)) & ={tan}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+3{cot}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & ={(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}))}^{2}+3{(\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}))}^{2} \\  & ={(\sqrt{3})}^{2}+3{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{2} \\  & =3+3(\frac{3}{9}) \\  & =3+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since cot(x)=cos(x)/sin(x), it approaches −∞ as x approaches π from the left and +∞ from the right. The one-sided limits differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, let's attempt to evaluate the limit by direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi }\operatorname{cot}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi } \\  & =\frac{-1}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13940317/assets/5e9d0e9d944cda9c97555ffdeac5aa245905f800cd99e11f5d172203bad3892d.png)

As $x$ approaches $\pi $ from the left, the values of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)$ are negative and decrease without bound. Therefore

$$
{lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)=-\infty 
$$

However, as $x$ approaches $\pi $ from the right, the values of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)$ are positive and grow without bound. Therefore

$$
{lim}_{x\to {\pi }^{+}}\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)=\infty 
$$

Since the two limits are not equal, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \pi }\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

decision.explanation: Substitute x=π: the angle is π/3−π/6=π/6. Since sin(π/6)=1/2, csc²(π/6)=1/(1/2)²=4.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\pi $ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi }{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & ={csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x) & =\operatorname{csc}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit of a Cosecant Function
content.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{3}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(2x) & =\operatorname{csc}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x)-\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})-\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}-\sqrt{3})}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{0}{1}-\sqrt{3})}{2} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}

content.worked_solution:
Substituting $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x)-\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\pi }{6})-\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}-\sqrt{3})}{2} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{0}{1}-\sqrt{3})}{2} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
